name: Air polishing (Airflow)
lead: Air polishing, often called by the brand-derived name Airflow, is a dental procedure in which a handpiece sprays a pressurised mix of water, air and fine powder onto the teeth to remove extrinsic stains and soft deposits such as plaque biofilm. It is performed by dentists and hygienists, usually during a cleaning visit, and is discussed in appearance circles as a way to lift coffee, tea, wine and tobacco staining without scraping.[1][2]

Dental sources describe it as part of the broader practice of polishing, which is mainly cosmetic and has limited therapeutic value on its own.[1] Traditional air polishing used sodium bicarbonate; lower-abrasion powders such as glycine and erythritol have since been studied, including for subgingival use around teeth and implants.[3][4][5]

Air polishing removes surface stain rather than changing the intrinsic colour of the tooth, which is what peroxide bleaching targets.[2] Research on the technique is concentrated on periodontal and implant maintenance rather than on cosmetic outcomes.

paras: A powder jet handpiece delivers warm water, compressed air and a fine abrasive or non-abrasive powder in a stream directed at the tooth surface. Wikipedia describes the older version as a prophy-jet spraying water and sodium bicarbonate that works well on extrinsic stains and soft deposits.[1]
Staining commonly comes from coffee, tea, red wine, smoking, chromogenic bacteria in plaque and some antimicrobial rinses, and polishing in general is used to remove it.[1]

Lower-abrasivity powders were developed so that the jet can be used below the gumline. A 2010 study examined subgingival plaque removal with a newer air-polishing device,[7] and reviews have discussed subgingival air polishing for periodontal biofilm infections.[5]
Systematic reviews have examined air polishing as an adjunct for peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis, the inflammatory conditions around dental implants.[8][9]

Published human research on air polishing is mostly clinical-periodontal rather than cosmetic. Reviews have assessed its efficacy in non-surgical treatment of peri-implant diseases and of periodontal biofilm infections,[5][8][9] and a consensus report on peri-implant disease care covers non-surgical treatment and maintenance.[10]

Registered trials listed on ClinicalTrials.gov include comparisons of trehalose versus glycine powder in peri-implant mucositis,[11] erythritol air polishing in peri-implantitis,[12] and a trial comparing bristle brush, rubber cup and air polishing for tooth surface roughness after scaling.[13] Several of these are recruiting or unreported, and results are not summarised here.

Wikipedia lists contraindications for sodium bicarbonate air polishing including sodium-restricted diets, hypertension, respiratory illness, infectious disease, chronic kidney disease and certain endocrine conditions or medications.[1] General polishing risks it describes include removal of the fluoride-rich outer enamel, frictional heat, scratching of restorations and gum trauma.[1]
A systematic review found that dental procedures generate droplets and aerosol, which is relevant to infection control.[6]

card.summary: A dentist's powder-jet cleaning that lifts surface stain; it changes surface colour, not the tooth's intrinsic shade.
card.aka: Airflow, powder jet polishing, air abrasion polishing
card.note: Contraindicated in some medical conditions; generates aerosol.

quick.overview:
Air polishing is a professional cleaning step where a handpiece sprays water, air and fine powder to remove stain and plaque from teeth. It is sometimes mentioned in teeth-appearance discussions as a stain-removal option.

Research on it centres on gum and implant care rather than cosmetics, so evidence for appearance outcomes specifically is limited.
quick.mechanism: A pressurised jet of powder (sodium bicarbonate, glycine or erythritol) and water abrades away extrinsic stain and soft biofilm from tooth surfaces.
quick.risks: Reported cautions include contraindications for people with sodium-restricted diets, hypertension, respiratory or kidney conditions, possible gum or surface effects, and aerosol generation during the procedure.
